pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Identify scientific methods such as recycling and composting used in waste management.
- Explain the scientific principles underlying the methods used in waste management.
- Conduct an audit of waste management methods in schools and assess the effectiveness of each.

pages.title: Why Waste Needs Scientific Management
pages.body: Waste that is simply dumped without any thought or treatment can pollute soil, water and air, spread disease, and permanently waste materials that could otherwise be reused. Scientific waste management applies systematic, evidence based methods to reduce the harm waste causes and, wherever possible, to recover value from it, rather than treating waste as something to be discarded and forgotten.

pages.title: Recycling
pages.body: Recycling is the scientific method of collecting used materials, such as plastic, glass, paper and metal, and processing them so they can be manufactured into new products, rather than being sent to a landfill. The scientific principle underlying recycling is that many materials retain useful physical or chemical properties even after their first use, meaning they can be melted, pulped, or otherwise reprocessed into raw material for new items, conserving natural resources and reducing the energy typically needed to produce materials from scratch.

pages.title: Composting
pages.body: Composting, studied in more agricultural detail in an earlier strand, is the scientific method of allowing organic waste, such as food scraps and plant matter, to decompose under controlled conditions with the help of bacteria, fungi and other decomposer organisms, producing a nutrient rich material that can improve soil fertility. The scientific principle underlying composting is the same biological process of decomposition that occurs throughout nature, deliberately managed and accelerated to safely convert organic waste into a useful product rather than allowing it to rot uncontrolled.

pages.title: Incineration
pages.body: Incineration is the controlled burning of waste at high temperature, reducing its volume substantially and, in some facilities, generating heat that can be converted into electricity. The scientific principle underlying incineration is combustion, a chemical reaction between the waste material and oxygen that releases energy as heat, though careful temperature control and filtering of resulting gases are needed to prevent harmful air pollution.

pages.title: Landfilling
pages.body:
Landfilling, though the least sophisticated of the methods discussed here, still involves scientific planning when done properly, since a well engineered landfill uses layers of compacted soil and impermeable lining material to contain waste and prevent it from contaminating surrounding soil and groundwater, alongside systems to manage the methane gas produced as buried organic waste slowly decomposes without oxygen.

[[pic:A four panel diagram showing the four waste management methods discussed, a recycling panel showing plastic bottles being sorted and melted into pellets, a composting panel showing food waste decomposing into dark soil, an incineration panel showing waste being burned in a controlled furnace with a filtered chimney, and a landfill panel showing a cross section of a properly lined and layered landfill site.]]

Notice how each method relies on a distinct scientific principle, the reusability of material properties in recycling, biological decomposition in composting, combustion in incineration, and controlled containment in landfilling, even though all four methods share the same broad goal of managing waste responsibly.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Conducting a School Waste Management Audit

pages.title: Conducting a School Waste Management Audit
pages.body: A waste management audit involves systematically observing and recording how waste is currently handled in a specific location, such as a school, identifying which methods, if any, are being used, and assessing how effectively each method is being applied. A thorough audit typically records the types and amount of waste generated, notes whether waste is being sorted for recycling or composting, observes final disposal methods, such as collection for landfill or open burning, and identifies clear opportunities for improvement based on the scientific methods studied in this lesson.

pages.title: The Scientific Principle Behind Each Method of Waste Management
pages.body:
| **METHOD** | **WHAT IS DONE** | **SCIENTIFIC PRINCIPLE** | **SUITABLE WASTE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recycling** | Waste is collected, sorted, cleaned and made into new products | A physical change. Plastics, glass and metals are melted and remoulded without becoming new substances | Plastic bottles, sachets, glass, metal cans, paper |
| **Composting** | Organic waste is heaped and allowed to rot in the presence of air | Decomposition by microorganisms that use oxygen. It gives humus, carbon (IV) oxide, water and heat | Food scraps, leaves, crop residues, animal droppings |
| **Biogas production** | Organic waste is sealed in a tank called a digester | Decomposition by microorganisms without oxygen. It gives methane gas for cooking and a slurry used as fertiliser | Animal dung, food waste, toilet waste |
| **Incineration** | Waste is burned at a very high temperature in a special furnace | Combustion. It greatly reduces the volume of waste and destroys germs, but the smoke must be cleaned | Hospital waste and other waste that cannot be recycled |
| **Landfilling** | Waste is spread in a lined pit, pressed down and covered with soil each day | Burial with slow decomposition. A lining stops polluted liquid from reaching ground water | Waste that is left after sorting |
| **Reuse** | An item is used again for the same or another purpose | No change to the material, so no energy is needed to remake it | Bottles, containers, bags, clothes |

When a school carries out a waste audit, the class records each type of waste produced in a week, weighs or counts it, notes how it is disposed of at present and judges each method by cost, safety, effect on the environment and how much waste it removes.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Many schools in Ghana are increasingly introducing designated bins for different types of waste, alongside school gardens that make direct use of compost produced from food waste, providing practical, everyday examples of the scientific waste management methods studied in this lesson being applied in a familiar setting.

lessons.title: Impact of Waste and Innovative Management for Sustainable Development

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain the impact of waste produced on the environment.
- Identify innovative ways to manage waste for sustainable development.
- Describe the types of waste produced within communities in Ghana.
- Examine and critique the waste management practices in Ghana, identifying positives, negatives and opportunities for improvement.

pages.title: Types of Waste Produced Within Communities in Ghana
pages.body: Organic waste, such as food scraps and plant matter, plastic waste, including bags, bottles and packaging, electronic waste, such as broken phones, batteries and old appliances, and construction waste, such as broken blocks and wood offcuts, are common types of waste produced across many Ghanaian communities, each requiring different handling and posing different environmental challenges.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Impact of Waste on the Environment

pages.title: The Impact of Waste on the Environment
pages.body: Polluting water bodies, contaminating soil, releasing harmful gases, and harming wildlife are four significant impacts poorly managed waste can have on the environment. Plastic waste dumped into rivers and drains can block waterways, contributing to flooding, and can be ingested by fish and other aquatic animals, harming them directly. Organic waste left to decompose in the open can attract disease carrying pests and release methane, a gas that contributes to climate change. Electronic waste, if not handled carefully, can leak harmful chemicals such as lead and mercury into soil and groundwater. Construction waste, though generally less chemically hazardous, can take up large amounts of land space and disrupt natural drainage patterns if not disposed of properly.

pages.title: Innovative Waste Management Technologies
pages.body:
Waste to energy plants, plastic recycling into building materials, and mobile phone based waste collection scheduling are examples of innovative technologies being explored and implemented to manage waste more sustainably. Waste to energy plants burn suitable waste under carefully controlled conditions to generate electricity, reducing landfill volume while producing usable power. Innovative building material recycling melts or compresses plastic waste into durable bricks, pavement tiles, or roofing materials, giving discarded plastic a genuinely useful second life. Mobile phone based scheduling systems allow households and waste collection companies to coordinate pickup times more efficiently, reducing uncollected waste accumulating in communities.

[[pic:A labelled infographic showing four types of waste (organic, plastic, electronic, construction) on the left, connected by arrows to a central label reading Innovative Waste Management, which branches out on the right to three labelled boxes, Waste to Energy Plants, Recycled Building Materials, and Mobile Collection Scheduling.]]

Notice how different types of waste can potentially be matched to different innovative management approaches, rather than assuming a single method could handle every type of waste a community produces.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Waste Management Practices in Ghana, An Honest Assessment

pages.title: Waste Management Practices in Ghana, An Honest Assessment
pages.body: Positives, negatives, and opportunities for improvement can all be identified when examining current waste management practices across Ghana. On the positive side, formal waste collection services operate in many urban areas, and public awareness of recycling and proper disposal has grown in recent years, alongside a small but active informal recycling sector that collects and sells materials such as scrap metal and plastic. On the negative side, waste collection remains inconsistent or absent in many communities, particularly in less urbanised areas, open dumping and burning of waste, including plastic, remains common, and formal recycling infrastructure is still limited compared with the volume of waste generated. Opportunities for improvement include expanding formal waste collection to more communities, investing further in recycling infrastructure and waste to energy technology, and strengthening public education about the environmental impact of poor waste disposal.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Community led initiatives, such as youth groups organising local clean up exercises or small businesses collecting plastic waste for resale to recyclers, show that meaningful improvement in waste management does not always require large scale government or corporate investment, and can begin with organised, motivated community action.
